name: Coit Tower
summary_en: Coit Tower's civic record centers on its fabric and its art. A 1989 Historic Structure Report, prepared for the Arts Commission, inventories the tower's exterior walls, the Columbus-statue planter, the tower shaft and the belvedere level for preservation. A 1989 guide to the city's Civic Art Collection places the tower's murals under the Arts Commission's aesthetic-review authority — no structure on public land, it notes, receives a building permit without that review. Recreation & Park Commission minutes from 1986, which index several Coit Tower resolutions, record the passage of the Prop. 43 Park Bond, an application to the state Office of Historic Preservation, and arrangements for groups to view the murals. The tower is operated by the Recreation & Parks Department, whose FY2025 department budget totals about $250M citywide.

ocr_excerpts: famous murals. The Commission's Civic Design Review authority is administered by its two architecture and one landscape architecture commissioners. No structure on public land may receive a building permit without the aesthetic review of the Arts Commission. The Commission's first historic case was the Coit Tower and the surrounding controversies over its existence and its design on Telegraph Hill. Although Coit Tower later became a distinctive San Francisco landmark, in the early years it was seen by many residents as a "blight" on the Telegraph Hill landscape and the style too "modern. " Even more controversial were the Coit Tower murals com- missioned by the federal government's Public Works of Art Program, a forerunner of the WPA arts program of the De- pression. Eight (of the twenty six) muralists, including Bernard Zakheim, John Langley Howard, Victor Arnautoff and others, were considered too "left leaning" and the structure

rmine and maintain the artist's original intent regarding the sculpture's appearance. Outdoor monuments are only one part of the city's collec- tion. Another great asset is the Works Progress Administration (WPA) artworks which were created during Franklin Roosevelt's term as president in the 1930s. The Coit Tower Murals hold a special place in the history of the era since they were the first to be funded under the Public Works of Art Project, (1933-34), the predecessor to the WPA program. Twenty-six artists plus their assistants were employed to create the murals at Coit Tower which depict life in California during the 1930's. Grants from the National Endowment for the Arts and the Office of Historic Preservation in Sacramento will allow the conservation of the murals to continue during the fall of 1988. velopment, and Supervisor Jane Kim’s Office) the Arts Commission held a Community Convening at the Art Institute in which over 60 community and culturai leaders discussed how to create meaningful change in the neighborhood with arts and culture at its core. san francisco arts commission Saving the Coit Tower Murals and the Civic Art Collection FISCAL YEAR 2011-12 ANNUAL REPORT For more information or to make a donation to ArtCare, please contact: Rachelle Axel, Development Director 415.252.2564 rachelle.axel@sfgov.org Established by voters in 1932, the San Francisco Arts Commission has jurisdiction over all of the art belonging to the City that are not included in the Asian Art or Fine Arts Museums collections. The City's Charter charges the Arts Commission with the preservation and care of the works in the Civic Art Collection. The murals located at Coit Tower are a part of this vast and prestigious collection, which today is comprised of over 4,000 objects. 800 of which are integrated into public facilities and spaces of every description, from the airport to the zoo. Collectively the Civic Art Collection is valued in excess of S93 million dollars. Due

maintenance/conservation budget for the entire collection was $75,000; prior to that it had only been $15,000 a year. Unfortunately, this amount is not enough to address the innumerable needs of an aging collection that is, in many cases, vulnerable to graffiti and other types of vandalism. Recently, Coit Tower has been in the news, because after 22 years and over 4 million visitors it is time for the Arts Commission to undertake significant restoration work on the murals. Created in 1934, the murals at Coit Tower include 27 distinct frescos painted by 26 artists, many of whom either studied with or were influenced by the famous Mexican muralists Diego Rivera and Jose Clemente Orozco.
